clinicalPearls: This is an umbrella group of several hundred genetic disorders affecting bone, cartilage, skin, tendons and other connective tissues; mutations in over 550 genes underlie 771 defined skeletal disorders, so classification by either clinical phenotype or causative gene remains a continuing challenge.

Connective tissue strength comes from fibrillar collagens (types I, II, III) whose alpha chains have a repeating Gly-X-Y sequence; glycine, the smallest amino acid, must occupy every third position, so substitution of glycine by a bulkier residue is a frequent disease-causing mechanism.

Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is dominated by bone fragility, deformity and growth deficiency; ~80-85% of cases stem from heterozygous COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations, and secondary features include blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, hearing loss, basilar invagination and cardiac-valve abnormalities.

OI bone is paradoxically hypermineralized: DXA returns a reduced density value, yet quantitative backscattered electron imaging and 3D CT show the bone is over-mineralized, making it both weak and brittle so that it snaps like chalk.

Null COL1A1 mutations (about half-normal but structurally normal collagen) produce mild type I OI, whereas structural glycine-substitution defects produce the more severe types II-IV; type II causes in-utero fractures and perinatal death.

The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (EDS) share soft hyperextensible skin, abnormal wound healing with atrophic/papyraceous scarring, easy bruising and joint hypermobility; the current classification recognizes 13 clinical types across roughly 20 genes.

Vascular EDS (COL3A1, type III collagen) is the dangerous form: medium- and large-vessel arterial rupture, sigmoid colon perforation without prior colon disease, and uterine rupture in the third trimester can occur, often in skin that is thin and translucent rather than velvety hyperextensible.
Classic EDS is most often due to COL5A1/COL5A2 (type V collagen) mutations in ~90% of patients; hypermobile EDS has no identified gene, so it remains a clinical diagnosis of exclusion.

Marfan syndrome (MFS) classically combines a tall marfanoid habitus with arachnodactyly, ectopia lentis (lens dislocation, ~60%), and aortic root dilation at the sinuses of Valsalva; ~95% of cases are due to fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutations.

FBN1 defects impair not only microfibril structure but also TGF-beta bioavailability; reduced/altered fibrillin-1 releases sequestered TGF-beta in the aortic wall, driving remodeling, excess MMP-2/MMP-9, and the aneurysmal phenotype.

Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGFBR1/2, TGFB2/3, SMAD2/3) overlaps with MFS but is distinguished by arterial tortuosity and aneurysms beyond the aortic root, hypertelorism, and cleft palate or bifid uvula; ectopia lentis is typically absent.
Achondroplasia, the common short-limb dwarfism, is caused by a gain-of-function FGFR3 mutation; most cases are sporadic, and the homozygous form is more severe and may be lethal in the neonate.
harrison.pathophysiology: Connective tissues (skin, bone, cartilage, ligament, tendon, vessel wall) are built from an extracellular matrix of fibrillar collagens, proteoglycans, elastin/fibrillin microfibrils and noncollagenous glycoproteins. Fibrillar collagen monomers are triple helices of alpha chains with a repeating Gly-X-Y motif; glycine at every third position is sterically required, and proline/hydroxyproline confer rigidity. Procollagen undergoes extensive post-translational processing (prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation requiring ascorbate, glycosylation, triple-helix folding aided by chaperones, secretion, N- and C-propeptide cleavage, then self-assembly into fibrils stabilized by lysyl-oxidase cross-links). Mutations may be quantitative (null alleles giving reduced normal collagen, generally milder) or structural (glycine substitutions, splice defects, charged/branched residue substitutions in X/Y positions) that disrupt folding, fibril assembly and mineralization. OI arises mainly from dominant type I collagen defects, plus rarer recessive defects in collagen modification, processing, folding/cross-linking and osteoblast differentiation. EDS reflects defects in collagen types I/III/V, in processing enzymes (ADAMTS2), cross-linking (PLOD1/lysyl hydroxylase 1), glycosaminoglycan biosynthesis, or matrix glycoproteins (tenascin X). Marfan/HTAD reflects fibrillin-1 microfibril dysfunction with secondary dysregulation of TGF-beta signaling; Loeys-Dietz reflects primary mutations in the TGF-beta pathway. Chondrodysplasias reflect intrinsic cartilage/growth-plate abnormalities (e.g., FGFR3 gain-of-function in achondroplasia, COL2A1 in type II collagenopathies).
additionalDifferentials: Postmenopausal or secondary osteoporosis (can mimic mild adult-onset OI)
Battered child syndrome / non-accidental injury (versus OI fractures in infants)
Other chondrodysplasias and skeletal dysplasias presenting with short stature
Homocystinuria (marfanoid habitus with ectopia lentis - lens dislocation typically downward)
Mucopolysaccharidoses and other lysosomal storage disorders
Acquired/secondary causes of joint hypermobility distinct from hereditary EDS
nonInfectiousMimics: Osteoporosis and osteopenia of other cause
Acromegaly (paw-like hand/foot enlargement of primary hypertrophic osteopathy can mimic it)
Secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy from pulmonary disease
Osteoarthritis (mild adult chondrodysplasia can resemble primary generalized OA)
Non-syndromic familial thoracic aortic aneurysm versus syndromic HTAD
additionalInvestigations: Targeted candidate-gene sequencing, multigene skeletal/EDS/HTAD panels, or whole-exome sequencing for molecular diagnosis
Skin fibroblast culture biochemistry for collagen synthesis/structure in selected cases
DXA bone densitometry (note it underestimates true mineral in OI; quantitative backscattered electron imaging or 3D CT reveals hypermineralization)
Skeletal radiographs (Wormian skull bones, popcorn metaphyses, beaded ribs, undertubulated long bones in OI)
Echocardiography for aortic root and valve assessment (MFS, LDS, and adults with OI)
Slit-lamp ophthalmologic examination for ectopia lentis in suspected MFS
Plasma amino acid analysis to exclude homocystinuria in marfanoid patients
Spirometry/pulmonary function testing in moderate-to-severe OI
Bone histomorphometry in selected diagnostically difficult OI cases
redFlags: Acute severe chest, back or abdominal pain in MFS/LDS or vascular EDS - possible aortic dissection or arterial rupture
Rapidly enlarging aortic root or sinus of Valsalva dilation on echocardiography
Spontaneous sigmoid colon perforation or organ rupture in vascular EDS
Uterine rupture in the third trimester (vascular EDS) and obstetric complications
Recurrent or in-utero fractures with progressive deformity (severe/lethal OI)
Progressive basilar invagination/impression with neurologic compromise in severe OI
Declining pulmonary function or recurrent pneumonia in severe OI (leading cause of death)
harrison.prognosis: Highly variable, even within a single disorder type and among family members carrying the same mutation. In OI, type I is mild and fractures often decline after puberty, while type II is lethal in the perinatal period; pulmonary disease is the leading cause of death in OI. In Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, cardiovascular disease (aortic dilation, dissection, rupture; mitral valve disease) is the major source of morbidity and mortality, and dilation rate is unpredictable and accelerated by exertion, emotional stress and pregnancy. Vascular EDS carries serious risk from arterial, intestinal and uterine rupture. Milder phenotypes across these disorders may go undiagnosed and have near-normal life expectancy.
pitfalls: DXA underestimates true bone mineral in OI - a low DXA value coexists with actual hypermineralization, so bone is brittle despite the reading.
Marfan-like presentation may actually be homocystinuria; always check plasma amino acids before settling on MFS.
Hypermobile EDS has no confirmed gene; it is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion and cannot be confirmed by genetic testing.
Same clinical OI subtype may be assigned different type labels over a patient's lifetime or among family members under clinical (versus genetic) classification.
Blue sclerae are not specific to OI - they occur in EDS, MFS and even healthy individuals; conversely severe neonatal OI with white sclerae suggests recessive prolyl 3-hydroxylation defects.
In infants, OI fractures may be mistaken for non-accidental injury (battered child syndrome).
Tissues in MFS/LDS and EDS are friable, complicating surgical repair.
harrison.severityClassification: Osteogenesis imperfecta is classified by the Sillence system (clinical/radiologic types I-IV: type I mildest with normal-quality but reduced collagen; type II perinatal lethal; type III progressively deforming; type IV mild-to-moderate) extended to genetic types V-XXII grouped by causative gene and mechanism. Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are classified into 13 clinical types (e.g., classic, vascular, hypermobile, arthrochalasia, dermatosparaxis, kyphoscoliotic) by clinical features, inheritance and molecular defect. Marfan syndrome diagnosis uses the revised Ghent nosology, emphasizing aortic root dilation/dissection and ectopia lentis as cardinal features plus a systemic score. Heritable thoracic aortic disease is divided into syndromic and nonsyndromic (familial thoracic aortic aneurysm) forms.
management: In osteogenesis imperfecta, use bisphosphonate therapy to reduce fracture frequency alongside orthopaedic fracture care and intramedullary rodding of deformed long bones
In Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, slow aortic root dilatation with beta-blockers or angiotensin receptor blockers and undertake prophylactic aortic root surgery once thresholds are reached
In Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, protect joints with physiotherapy and bracing, and provide meticulous skin and wound care with tension-free closure and delayed suture removal
Supportive care including dental review for dentinogenesis imperfecta, audiology and hearing aids for hearing loss, and low-vision or lens support for ectopia lentis
Structured surveillance with serial echocardiography for aortic and valve disease, bone densitometry, ophthalmology and audiology as dictated by the specific disorder
Advise activity modification with avoidance of contact and high-impact sport to reduce fracture and vascular rupture risk
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across genetics, orthopaedics, cardiology and rehabilitation, and offer genetic counselling with cascade family screening
